Task 5 must delete a catalog entry only after the cleanup marker and cleanup-item retirement are durable, and must prune the namespace cursor before deleting the entry.

The C1 frontier fix removes both probing and durable holds for an uncataloged namespace because all probe and hold operations are reachable only inside the catalog-resolved loop.

The persisted fold cursor is keyed only by namespace and shard, so a recreated namespace can inherit a predecessor incarnation's sequence boundary and omit the new incarnation's first positive owner edges from the GC baseline.

The `RemovalReady` protocol is adopted as a transient catalog state between `Removing` and entry deletion: it is entered only after the terminal record has folded and the life-scoped cleanup item is durably `Completed`.
A `RemovalReady` namespace is excluded from GC walking and cursor creation, making cursor absence monotone while the catalog row remains present.

The `RemovalReady` predicate must be enforced at five cursor or walk producers: the catalog-only frontier loop, parent-cursor carry, hint admission, REBUILD, and the `Removing` to `RemovalReady` no-hold precondition.
The `Removing` to `RemovalReady` transition must refuse while a hold with `ShardCoverage::classification == 4` exists for the namespace.

A GC round whose catalog cut predates the `Removing` to `RemovalReady` CAS may write the cursor once more; the next round must prune it, and final deletion must revalidate the adopted seal and tolerate this one stale-cut round.

The mandatory catalog design treats an absent or undecodable `cas/ref_catalog` after pool initialization as `CORRUPTED_DATA` and stops creation, removal, and GC instead of interpreting it as a virgin empty catalog.

After `_cleanup` and the cleanup item are gone, legal removal debris and fabricated catalog-entry loss can be byte-identical, so an anomaly classifier cannot accept one and reject the other without another durable evidence object.

Canonical cursors for namespaces absent from the catalog are retired metadata and should be omitted from the next seal, while the condition is counted and logged rather than used for pool-wide suppression.
Deleting the perpetual `_files` janitor would make a single omitted `LIST` result leak dead-incarnation files permanently, because the one bounded cleanup attempt would be their only reclaimer.
The removal design must retain a negative test proving that cleanup failure or `_files` residue does not gate lifecycle completion, even when the bounded pass performs a best-effort `_files` listing.

A corrupt terminal record under the proposed removal protocol leaves the cleanup item `Pending`, prevents `RemovalReady`, and permanently wedges the name until `FORCE REBUILD` or decommission intervenes.
The stuck-removal observability path must surface a `Pending` item wedged by an unreadable terminal, including the actor that can unstick it and the operator-visible recovery state.

The catalog remains the authoritative namespace universe because a single token-CAS `GET` supplies one complete object-version cut, whereas stitched paginated `LIST` results need not represent any namespace set at one instant.
The captured LIST-incompleteness evidence establishes that a multi-page enumeration can omit durable objects, but does not identify the store-side mechanism or establish the behavior on AWS S3.

A bounded re-`LIST` or retry triggered by an out-of-order key cannot replace catalog authority because finite scans can agree while omitting an entire namespace and therefore produce no retry trigger.

`CasRefCatalog` should own namespace lifecycle decisions through typed operations such as `lookup`, `liveAndRemoving`, `ensureLive`, and `beginRemoval`, rather than exposing raw catalog rows to callers.
GC, ref cleanup, namespace cleanup, fsck, and decommission should consume one immutable `GcNamespacePlan` or one shared catalog snapshot and must not independently re-read catalog state.
The recorded S3 lane had 137 of 250 timeout lines naming `cas/ref_catalog` across 66 namespaces.
Permanent exact-`RootNamespace` non-reuse would avoid generation-based aliasing only by refusing supported exact-name reuse workflows, including shadow names and explicit UUID replay.
A permanent `Retired` catalog history grows with every historical namespace and eventually makes legitimate admissions return `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`; normal `Atomic` UUID churn does not bound that history.
`CasRefCatalog::read` currently treats an absent catalog as a virgin empty catalog, so a permanent `Retired`-only design would allow catalog loss after `_ckpt` deletion to reopen a name for birth.
Normal `Atomic` recreation creates a fresh table UUID and therefore a fresh namespace; it does not wait for the prior namespace to be removed.
`ATTACH TABLE ... UUID '<same>'` and explicit-UUID `CREATE TABLE` can reuse an old `RootNamespace`, and replicated database recovery can depend on preserving shared explicit UUIDs.
A shadow backup namespace is derived from its literal shadow directory, so reusing a shadow name reaches the same `RootNamespace`.

The final recommendation is to keep `NamespaceLifeId` and incarnation-qualified ref and namespace-file keys, avoid permanent `Retired` history and extra retirement markers, and delete a catalog entry only after terminal fold, cleanup/cursor retirement, and exact `_ckpt` deletion ordering is complete.

The Stage B strategic review found that catalog authority and incarnation protect different failure classes: the catalog closes hidden-universe ownership loss, while incarnation makes stale physical debris and deposed-writer writes inert across removal and rebirth.
The observed LIST omission was within a single enumeration call rather than explainable solely by cross-page snapshot isolation; its recency bound and RustFS mechanism remain unknown.

The catalog's advantage over LIST is atomic completeness as of one object-version cut, not freshness; protocol closes staleness after the cut but cannot recover a namespace never named by an incomplete LIST.

`existsFile` on a never-born namespace can mint a catalog entry and publish `_ckpt` from a read path, multiplying writes to the pool-wide catalog; `dropNamespace`, `listRefs`, and `resolveRef` were also identified as recover-and-mint paths.
`createNamespace` is the only production incarnation mint site, and stale-creator reconciliation changes only `creator` while leaving `state` and `incarnation` unchanged.

The incarnation is retained because temporary refusal alone cannot make omitted old physical objects safe for eventual same-name reuse; the generation makes old ref objects and namespace files structurally inert.
The earlier claim that same-name refusal would burn stateless CI lanes was retracted: under `Atomic`, drop-and-recreate uses a fresh table UUID and does not collide with the old namespace.

An immortal `Retired` row makes the catalog `O(historical namespaces)` on the hot full-object CAS path and eventually exhausts the catalog's admission budget; exact compaction is unavailable for arbitrary opaque names.
Stock `RESTORE` generates a fresh coordinated UUID, so it is not an exact-`RootNamespace` reuse route; shadow-name reuse and explicit-UUID replay remain supported reuse routes.

The precise incarnation debris scope is `_log`, `_snap`, `_ckpt`, and `_files`; part manifests retain `(namespace, mount-epoch, build-sequence)` identity and loose mountpoint objects are not incarnation-qualified.
Forbidding `Ordinary` with CAS would break replicated recovery because the broken-tables path deliberately creates an `Ordinary` database to discard a table UUID.
A `Removing` namespace with no terminal record must be surfaced after a configured number of GC rounds; GC must append nothing while it is stuck.

Creation during `Removing` or while a cleanup item is unretired must return a typed retryable refusal naming the wait, never `LOGICAL_ERROR`; creation succeeds and mints a fresh incarnation after entry removal.
Cleanup must capture `NamespaceLifeId` at deposition and never re-derive it from the catalog during a resumed or stale pass.

After `_cleanup` is removed, a legal removal and fabricated entry loss can both appear as an absent catalog entry with surviving canonical life-qualified debris, so the two cases cannot be separately classified from store contents alone.
A CREATE-side targeted lifecycle assist is a possible latency optimization, but it must use the normal durable terminal, cleanup, retirement, and cursor-pruning protocol and cannot bypass it.

The `RemovalReady` state machine is `Creating -> Live -> Removing -> RemovalReady -> absent`; `RemovalReady` means no writer publication, recovery, ref fold, or new cursor is permitted, and only exact removal of the row is legal.
`RemovalReady` is transient rather than a permanent tombstone, so it remains charged in catalog and fold-seal capacity reservations until the cleanup item and cursor are both retired.
Only the owning writer or a successor that has claimed and fenced the same server root may append `RemoveNamespace`; GC must never invent the terminal record.
A deposited cleanup item stores `NamespaceLifeId` and `remove_txn_id`, and every resumed or stale cleanup pass uses those captured values directly.

A pending cleanup item performs one bounded, suppression-aware, best-effort pass with exact-token deletion; `NotFound`, token mismatch, or LIST omission retains or defers work and never becomes a safety conclusion.

Terminal-owned manifests are cleaned from exact `ManifestId` values in the terminal record after decrements are durable; the removal pass does not LIST and delete the shared manifest namespace prefix.

A removal lifecycle must not require physical emptiness: omitted `_files` listings may leak bytes, but ref objects and namespace files are life-qualified and cannot affect later visibility or rebirth.
GC may CAS `Removing` to `RemovalReady` only when the matching cleanup item is durably `Completed`; it must not infer completion merely from item absence.
A `RemovalReady` round does not probe, fold, carry, or recreate the namespace cursor, and removes the matching completed cleanup item and shard-0 cursor together in the adopted seal.

Final removal requires the exact expected `RemovalReady` catalog row, an absent matching cleanup item, and an absent name-keyed shard-0 cursor; it then exact-deletes `_ckpt` and exact-CAS-deletes the complete observed row.

The `_cleanup` marker can be removed because stale cleanup targets only the deposited life-qualified ref and `_files` prefixes or exact old terminal-owned manifests, never a namespace-wide prefix that a new life can create.
A fresh catalog, life, and fence validation is still required immediately before every destructive delete even though deposited life identity provides the primary stale-pass isolation.

Canonical life-qualified objects whose life is not the current catalog life are inert debris; malformed or unparseable keys remain anomalies; an absent or undecodable initialized Stage-B catalog stops creation, removal, and GC.
Pool bootstrap must create the empty `cas/ref_catalog` before marking the Stage-B format ready, after which missing catalog reads cannot be treated as an empty catalog.
The catalog admission reservation must cover non-per-namespace seal data such as `blob_target_runs` and `condemned_summary`; entry ordering does not remove those capacity terms.

For a name in `Removing` or `RemovalReady`, creation returns a typed retryable error stating that terminal fold, cleanup completion, and cursor retirement are pending; a DROP-driven targeted fold is not part of the correctness baseline.
Deleting a catalog entry immediately after folding the terminal record permits multiple cleanup items for repeated lives of one name and breaks the fold-seal reservation bound.

The Stage B catalog is the sole authority for namespace lives, LIST is only a zero-trust hint, held `NamespaceLifeId` handles make hot reads catalog-free, destructive actions revalidate exact catalog tokens per key, and the destructive gate opens only on a complete catalog-proven frontier.
A `NamespaceLifeId` may originate only from catalog snapshot resolution; it must never be minted from a `RootNamespace`, LIST key, or path.
An absent canonical life is inert debris and must never become a pool-suppressing damage anomaly.
Held ref readers and lists must perform zero catalog GETs; a stale handle may see stale data or `NotFound`, but never a newer incarnation or a catalog-fence rejection caused solely by the hot read.
Ref mutations may require an admission or authority catalog snapshot because mutations are not hot reads.

Current-life destructive cleanup must revalidate the exact life, catalog-entry token, and fence immediately before every per-key `deleteExact`; a token change before the first delete permits no delete, while a change between two deletes refuses the second.
Within one operation, multiple life resolutions must use the same `CasRefCatalog::Snapshot` and must not observe different catalog snapshots.
The three publication effects are ordered as durable snapshot body, advanced `_ckpt`, and in-memory adoption; `Poisoned` refuses publication and triggers re-recovery.

Decommission selects victim namespaces by exact catalog ownership with no LIST fallback; `Removing` with `_ckpt` resumes the terminal append, `Removing` without `_ckpt` is `CORRUPTED_DATA`, and a proved-complete `Removing` row remains GC-owned.

Writer cleanup duties own precommit-owner settlement and the active-build-floor pin, not physical body deletion; settlement order is exact `OwnerTransition` append or conclusive absence, then `retireBuildSeq`, then duty removal, with failures retaining the duty for retry.

Physical unreachable bodies from `Rejected`, `Uncertain`, and `Durable` attempts remain GC/orphan-sweep-owned; the writer path never exact-deletes a body, and missing attribution suppresses destructive fallback.

The destructive gate formula is `frontier_complete = universe_authoritative && frontier_namespaces > 0 && frontier_proven == frontier_namespaces` and `suppress_destructive = anomalies || carried_holds || !frontier_complete`.

The destructive gate has five independent suppressors: non-empty anomalies, non-empty carried holds, `!universe_authoritative`, `frontier_namespaces == 0`, and `frontier_proven != frontier_namespaces`.
Enabling production destruction may change only the source of `frontier_complete` from hard-wired false to catalog-proven true; changing any other suppressor term is a protocol error.
